How it works

How the moving cost calculator works

You answer the same questions a mover would ask first. The calculator turns them into a realistic price range for your move.

There's no sign-up and no email gate. If the estimate looks right and you want a firm number, you can ask a specialist to confirm it. If not, you leave with a useful number and nothing else.

What you tell us

  • What you're moving: a home, office, piano, hot tub and more
  • Your moving-from and moving-to ZIP codes
  • Home size or item type
  • Roughly when you're moving
  • Any extras: packing, storage, car shipping

What you get back

  • A starting price for a move like yours
  • The distance, and whether it counts as local or long distance
  • A clear split between the move and optional extras
  • The option to get your exact price from a specialist

Price factors

What affects the cost of your move

Six things decide most of what you'll pay. Knowing them helps you read any quote and spot where you can save.

  • Distance

    Local moves are priced by time, long-distance moves mostly by miles and weight. Crossing state lines also brings federal rules into play.

    Big impact

  • How much you're moving

    More rooms means more weight, a bigger truck and more hours. Clearing out before the move is the easiest way to save.

    Big impact

  • Your moving date

    Summer, weekends and month-ends are busiest. A flexible date can lower the price.

    Medium impact

  • Stairs and access

    Flights of stairs, elevators, long walks from the truck or tight streets all add time.

    Medium impact

  • Heavy or delicate items

    Pianos, pool tables, hot tubs and safes need extra crew, special equipment and care.

    Varies

  • Packing and extras

    Packing, storage and car shipping are optional. Add only what you need.

    Optional

The cost to move a piano is about $220–$490 for an upright and $420–$1,100 for a grand on a local move of 10 road miles. Over 1,000 road miles, the cost to move a piano rises to about $1,050–$2,050 for an upright and $1,550–$3,200 for a grand. Each range assumes an off-peak date, no stairs and no extras; stairs, the mover you pick and damage cover change it.

Upright or grand: the cost to move a piano by type

The type of piano decides most of the cost to move a piano, because it sets the crew, the gear and the time on site. These are the calculator's ranges for each type, off peak, with no stairs at either end and no extras.

PianoLocal, 10 road milesLong distance, 1,000 road miles
Upright$220–$490$1,050–$2,050
Grand or baby grand$420–$1,100$1,550–$3,200

Why a grand costs more

An upright rolls out standing up, on a dolly. A grand has to come apart first. The movers take off the legs and the pedal lyre, and often the lid, then turn the body onto its straight side, strap it to a padded piano board and wheel it out. That takes more time, more hands and more gear, and the cost to move a piano follows the work. As a rule of thumb, an upright needs at least two movers and a grand at least three.

Size matters within each type

The weight guide at piano.org puts most acoustic pianos at 300 to 1,000 pounds. A tall full upright can weigh more than a baby grand, so give the mover the height of an upright or the length of a grand when you ask for a quote. In the calculator, spinets, consoles and studio pianos all count as uprights. If you aren't sure what you have, choose Not sure and the estimate covers either type.

Stairs, tight turns and the cost to move a piano

Stairs work differently in the cost to move a piano than in a household move. Boxes go up a flight one at a time; a piano goes up in one piece, strapped to a board and moved a step at a time by the whole crew. The calculator asks whether the job has no stairs, a few steps or full flights, and adds a set amount for them, more for a grand than for an upright. Count the stairs at both ends before you answer.

Before you ask for a quote, walk the route the piano will take and write down:

  • every step at each end, including porch and entry steps;
  • any turn or landing on the stairs, and how wide it is;
  • the narrowest doorway and hallway on the way out and on the way in;
  • an elevator, and whether the building makes movers book it;
  • a long walk from the truck, or grass, gravel or a steep driveway to cross.

Where no route works, such as an upper floor with a tight stairwell, a piano may have to be hoisted through a window or over a balcony. A mover prices that on top of the cost to move a piano, after seeing the site.

Piano movers or general movers?

A general moving crew can often handle an upright on a ground floor. For a grand, a flight of stairs or an instrument you value, a specialist piano mover is the safer choice, with a piano board, straps, a padded dolly and practice at taking a grand apart and putting it back together. Whoever you hire, ask:

  • How many pianos like mine have you moved?
  • Who takes off and refits a grand's legs and pedals?
  • How is the piano secured in the truck, and is it crated or blanket-wrapped for a long trip?
  • What cover comes with the price, and what does more cover cost?

Get every answer in writing with the quote, so you can compare the cost to move a piano between movers on the same terms.

Tuning after the move

Plan to have the piano tuned once it's in place. The new room matters as much as the trip: wood and strings shift as they settle into a different humidity and temperature, and the pitch drifts with them. A common rule of thumb is to wait a few weeks after delivery before the tuner comes, so the tuning holds.

Tuning isn't part of a mover's quote or of the cost to move a piano that the calculator shows, so budget for it on its own. Place the piano away from heating vents, radiators and sunny windows to help it hold its tune.

Damage cover for a valuable piano

A fine instrument can be worth many times the cost to move a piano, so settle the cover before moving day. On a move between states, federal law and the FMCSA's household goods rules (49 CFR Part 375) make the mover offer you two levels of liability. The FMCSA sets them out in its guide to valuation and insurance options.

Released value costs nothing extra, but the mover pays no more than $0.60 per pound per article. It pays by weight, not by worth, so for a valuable piano the payout would be a small share of what the piano is worth. You get it only if you sign a statement choosing it on the bill of lading.

Full-value protection is what you get if you don't sign for released value. The mover must repair the piano, replace it with a similar one, or pay the cost of the repair or its current replacement value, up to the value declared for the shipment. Typical published figures from moving-cost guides put its price at $10.00–$20.00 per $1,000 of declared value; the exact price and any deductible vary by mover. That price comes on top of the cost to move a piano that the calculator shows.

When the piano is your whole shipment, the shipment's value is the piano's, so declare what it would cost to replace. For an older or rare instrument, a written appraisal from a piano technician helps you set that value and supports a claim if one is needed.

Within one state, the federal rules don't apply, and state rules decide what a mover must offer. Whether the move is local or crosses state lines, get the mover's cover in writing alongside the cost to move a piano, and check whether your home insurance covers the piano while it's in transit.

From estimate to exact price

Five ways to get a quote you can count on

An estimate tells you what to expect. These steps make sure the final bill matches it.

Based on FMCSA moving guidance

  1. List your big items

    Beds, sofas, appliances and anything heavy. They drive weight, crew size and time.

  2. Ask for a survey

    An in-home or video walk-through gives the mover what they need to firm up the price.

  3. Get it in writing

    Know whether your estimate is binding or non-binding before you sign anything.

  4. Check the USDOT number

    For interstate moves, confirm the mover is registered with the FMCSA.

  5. Choose your coverage

    Decide between basic released value and full value protection before moving day.

Released value or full cover for your piano

Enter your piano's weight and what it's worth to see what each level of cover would pay if it broke on a move between states. Cover can matter more than the cost to move a piano itself.

If your $3,000 upright piano is broken, basic cover pays $180.

Released value, the basic cover a mover includes at no charge, pays at most 60 cents a pound for each item. Full-value protection pays to repair or replace it, up to its value. The released rate is the Surface Transportation Board's, and a mover may raise it each year. Full-value protection is the default: a mover's estimate must include it, and your goods move under it unless you give it up in writing. Under it, a mover may pay at most $100 a pound for an item worth more than $100 a pound, such as jewelry, unless you list the item in writing.

Released value pays $180

Full-value protection pays up to $3,000

Full-value protection is priced on the whole shipment: about $10.00–$20.00 per $1,000 of declared value.

Questions

Piano moving cost FAQ

Can't find your answer? Email hello@liftmyboxes.com.

What is the cheapest way to move a piano?

To cut the cost to move a piano, book an off-peak date, clear the route before the crew arrives and, if you're moving house anyway, ask whether adding the piano to the household move costs less than a separate trip. Doing it yourself saves the mover's fee, but piano.org's moving guide says it isn't a do-it-yourself job, because a piano weighs hundreds of pounds and is easily damaged. A cracked soundboard or a hurt helper can cost far more than the move.

Why do so many people give pianos away for free?

Often because the cost to move a piano is more than an old upright would sell for. A free piano still needs movers, so expect to pay for the move yourself: about $220–$490 for an upright going 10 road miles with no stairs. Have a piano technician look it over before you accept it, so you don't pay to move an instrument that can't be tuned or repaired.

Is an old upright piano worth moving?

It depends on the make, the condition and what replacing it would cost you. A piano technician can check the soundboard, pin block and action and tell you roughly what it's worth. Set what it's worth against the cost to move a piano like it, from the calculator above. If it needs repairs that cost more than it's worth, selling or donating it may make more sense than moving it.

What is the cost to move a piano across the country?

At 1,000 road miles, an upright costs about $1,050–$2,050 to move and a grand about $1,550–$3,200, off peak with no stairs. A coast-to-coast trip is far longer than that, so the cost to move a piano that far is higher, though each extra mile adds less on a long route. Enter both ZIP codes in the calculator above to price your exact route.

Does a digital piano cost as much to move?

No. The weight guide at piano.org puts a digital piano at 25 to 150 pounds, against hundreds of pounds for an acoustic one, so it needs no piano board or specialist crew. Move it like any other piece of furniture, in its original box if you kept it. It never needs tuning after the trip.
